summary.text: Phytoplankton are the self-feeding part of the plankton: microscopic photosynthesizing bacteria and protists living in the sunlit upper layer of oceans and lakes.
Though they make up only about 1% of global plant biomass, they account for about half of global photosynthesis and at least half of oxygen production.
They form the base of marine and freshwater food webs, and besides light they depend on nutrients such as nitrate, phosphate and trace metals like iron.

facts.label: Turnover time
facts.value: Days, versus decades for land plants

facts.label: Main members
facts.value: Cyanobacteria and single-celled protists such as diatoms

facts.label: Southern Ocean limit
facts.value: Often short of the micronutrient iron

items.prompt: Phytoplankton make up only about 1% of the world's plant biomass. What share of global photosynthetic activity do they account for?

options.label: About 1%
About 10%
About half
Over 90%

items.explain: Despite their small biomass, phytoplankton carry out about half of global photosynthetic activity.

items.prompt: Why do phytoplankton crowd into the upper layer of an ocean or lake rather than the deep?

options.label: They need light to make their food
Deep water is too salty for them
Their predators all live in the deep
Cold water deeper down freezes them

items.explain: Phytoplankton get energy by photosynthesis, so they must live in the well-lit surface layer, the euphotic zone.

items.prompt: In large experiments, scientists added iron salts to stretches of ocean. What were they hoping to achieve?

options.label: Make the water less acidic for corals
Boost plankton to pull carbon dioxide from the air
Poison algae blooms that kill fish
Make seawater dense enough to sink

items.explain: Phytoplankton are often limited by iron, so adding it aims to promote their growth and draw atmospheric CO₂ into the ocean.

items.prompt: Why do phytoplankton react to climate swings across the globe much faster than forests do?

options.label: They can swim toward better conditions
They are larger than most trees
They only live near the equator
Their populations turn over in days

items.explain: Phytoplankton turn over in days rather than decades, so they respond rapidly to climate variations on a global scale.

items.prompt: A drifting single cell photosynthesizes but also swallows other microbes. Why do scientists no longer file it simply under phytoplankton?

options.label: It is too large to count as plankton
It can swim against strong currents
Because it also eats, it counts as mixoplankton
It only lives in fresh water

items.explain: Groups like dinoflagellates that are phototrophic but also eat other organisms are now termed mixoplankton rather than phytoplankton.

items.prompt: A boater spots a large coloured patch on the sea surface made of countless microscopic drifting cells. What gives the patch its colour?

options.label: Sunlight bouncing off sand below
Chlorophyll and other pigments in the cells
Oil released by schools of fish
Salt crystals forming at the surface

items.explain: In large enough numbers, phytoplankton can tint the surface because of chlorophyll and, in some species, accessory pigments.
